title: Payment API latency spike
executive_summary: INC-001 (SEV2): Payment API latency spike. Checkout took 3-5 seconds and some payments failed with 5xx errors from 14:00Z. The investigation status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED, and the critic approved the result. The leading hypothesis (H1, confidence 0.63) is database connection pool exhaustion in payment-service. Connections held by RefundService.processPartialRefund filled payment-db-pool, so payment calls queued, timed out after 5 seconds, and returned errors. Leak-detection warnings for connections held over 30 seconds by RefundService began at 13:45Z (payment-service logs). Payment-service db_conn_util_pct rose from about 35% before any latency change (critic review; 52% at 13:50Z, 78% at 13:55Z, 96% at 14:00Z). At 14:00:16Z the pool reached active=50, idle=0, with up to 98 waiters, and the timeout errors began (logpat-payment-service-7d1739af). Payment-service P95 latency rose from a 150 ms baseline to a window mean of 1315 ms, and error rate rose from 0.8% to 9.9% from 14:00Z (met-payment-service-p95_latency_ms, met-payment-service-error_rate). API gateway 503s followed at 14:01Z (logpat-api-gateway-2be6bd23). Request rate was flat (about 302 req/s), so the cause is a holding problem, not load. The hypotheses that Postgres report_rollup contention (H2) and the notification-service 3.4.1 deployment (H3) caused the incident were rejected. The trigger that started the RefundService connection hold has not been identified, so this is the most probable explanation at the category and culprit level, not a fully confirmed mechanism.

critic_review.summary: H1 is the best-supported hypothesis: connection-pool exhaustion in payment-service caused by connections held by RefundService.processPartialRefund. Independent checks support it. Payment-service's own db_conn_util_pct rose from a ~35% baseline starting at 13:49Z (52% at 13:50, 78% at 13:55, 96% at 14:00), before any latency or error change. Leak-detection warnings for RefundService holds >30s recur from 13:45Z onward. Pool exhaustion (active=50, idle=0, waiting up to 98) begins at 14:00:16Z, coinciding with the P95 and error-rate step at 14:00:00Z. The gateway 503s start at 14:01Z, downstream of this. Request rate is flat, which fits a holding problem rather than load. The 15-minute lead is explained by gradual pool depletion, not a timing contradiction. H2 is rejected: Postgres CPU, p95 and disk IO are flat, the report_rollup statements are not attributed to the payment pool, and the application logs attribute the held connections to RefundService. H3 is rejected: notification-service is not in payment-service's dependency graph, there is no shared-resource evidence, and the SMTP throttling predates the deployment. Limitation: the trigger that began the RefundService connection hold (the partial-refund path leaking or stalling) is not yet identified; this is a deeper cause and does not block approval of the category and culprit.

assessments.reasoning: Payment-service pool utilisation climbs from 13:49Z, before the 14:00Z onset. Leak warnings attribute held connections to RefundService.processPartialRefund from 13:45Z. Pool saturation errors match exactly at 14:00:16Z, with P95, error and timeout steps at 14:00Z and flat request rate. Gateway 503s are downstream. Postgres-side utilisation is consistent with the same sessions.

Postgres CPU (+1%), p95 latency (+0.7%) and disk IO wait (-0.8%) are flat, which contradicts DB-side saturation or lock contention. The report_rollup statements are not linked to the payment pool. The application attributes the held connections to RefundService, not to report sessions.

No topology path exists between notification-service and payment-service or order-service. There is no metric or log evidence of shared resource impact. SMTP throttling began before the 13:54Z deployment. The timing correlation is weak and the payment-side leak evidence points elsewhere.

The trigger that started the RefundService connection hold at ~13:45Z is not explained.
alternative_explanations: report_rollup contention on Postgres (H2): contradicted by flat DB CPU, latency and IO wait.
notification-service side effect (H3): no dependency path and no resource-level evidence.
Organic load increase: request rate is flat, so this is contradicted.

probable_root_cause.description: Connections leaked by RefundService.processPartialRefund exhaust payment-db-pool, so checkout payment calls queue, time out and return 5xx.
probable_root_cause.label: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence)

root_cause_statement: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence): db_connection_pool_exhaustion in payment-service - Connections leaked by RefundService.processPartialRefund exhaust payment-db-pool, so checkout payment calls queue, time out and return 5xx.
corrective_actions: Immediately release the connections held by RefundService.processPartialRefund (for example, recycle the payment-service instances or the affected pool connections) to restore free capacity in payment-db-pool. Confirm recovery by checking that active connections fall below 50 and waiters reach zero.
If leaks recur, temporarily disable or throttle the partial-refund path so it stops consuming payment-db-pool connections, while keeping checkout payments running.

Confirm which sessions hold the connections by querying pg_stat_activity during the incident window. The critic noted that exclusive attribution to RefundService was inferred from application logs and not verified (evidence gap to close).
Watch for recovery in payment-service P95, error rate, and timeout rate, and for the api-gateway 503 rate, since these lagged the pool exhaustion.
preventive_actions: Find and fix the code path in RefundService.processPartialRefund that leaves connections checked out or stalls while holding them. Make sure every connection is released in a finally block or try-with-resources, and that no external call is made while a connection is held.

Set a maximum connection hold time and a statement or transaction timeout on the payment pool so a single caller cannot hold connections indefinitely. Consider separate pools for refund and checkout traffic so refunds cannot starve payments.
Add regression tests or load tests for the partial-refund flow that check connections are returned after success, failure, and timeout.
Review the report_rollup long-running statements (18 seconds in logs) separately as a performance hygiene item, even though they were not the cause of this incident.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert when payment-db-pool active connections stay at or near the max (for example, above 80% for 2 minutes) or when waiting threads are above zero for more than 1 minute.
Alert on HikariPool connection leak-detection warnings (payment-service logs), and page on any hold longer than 30 seconds attributed to RefundService.
Track payment-service db_conn_util_pct per service and alert on a sustained rise above the roughly 35-40% baseline, since this rise preceded the latency change by about 15 minutes.

Keep alerts on payment-service P95 latency (baseline about 150 ms), error rate (baseline about 1%), timeout rate, and api-gateway upstream 503 counts, and add a dashboard that correlates these with pool metrics.
Log the source service or operation name on connection acquisition and timeout events, so pool owners can be identified without manual database queries.
limitations: Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
Investigation terminated because: critic verdict APPROVED
conclusion: The incident is best explained by connection pool exhaustion in payment-service, caused by connections held by RefundService.processPartialRefund. The mechanism is supported by application logs, metrics, and the timing of the pool-saturation event relative to the latency and error onset. The rejected alternatives (Postgres report_rollup contention and the notification-service deployment) are contradicted by the available evidence. Two gaps remain: the trigger that began the connection hold around 13:45Z is unexplained, and connection ownership has not been verified in pg_stat_activity. Mitigation should focus on releasing the held connections and preventing recurrence through leak fixes, hold-time limits, and pool isolation for refund traffic.
